judgments.catchwords: MONEYLENDING - Unlicensed moneylending - Loan disguised as sale of land - Sale and purchase agreement and irrevocable power of attorney - Whether transaction constituted genuine sale or loan at interest secured by land - Advance of RM200,000 with additional repayment of RM60,000 - Six-month repayment arrangement - Substantial disparity between stated purchase price and land value - Assessment of transaction’s true character from terms and surrounding circumstances - Presumption of carrying on business of moneylending upon proof of single loan at interest - Whether presumption rebutted - Instruments declared void and unenforceable - Moneylenders Act 1951, ss 15 and 100A - Contracts Act 1950, s 24(b). judgments.title: YAP CHENG CHAI v Pendakwa Raya
judgments.catchwords: CRIMINAL LAW: Penal Code — Section 457 read with Section 34 — Daytime housebreaking with intent to commit theft — Elements of offence — Distinction between lurking house-trespass (s. 443) and housebreaking (s. 445) — Requirement of proving house-trespass (s. 442) — Allegation of acting in concert with two accomplices at large — Whether prosecution proved substantive offence and common intention beyond reasonable doubt. CRIMINAL LAW: Common Intention — Section 34 Penal Code — Constructive liability — Pre-arranged plan and concerted action — Test in Mahbub Shah v Emperor and Namasiyiam Doraisamy v PP — Prosecution's failure to produce neighbour’s CCTV depicting getaway car and accomplices — Internal CCTV (Exhibit P12) showing only a single perpetrator — Presence of unmatched fourth fingerprint (J4) on outer gate — Whether common intention established — Whether failure to prove common intention renders charge fatally defective where substantive offence can be proved individually — Section 34 as a rule of joint liability rather than a standalone substantive offence. EVIDENCE: Computer-Generated Evidence — CCTV recording — Section 90A Evidence Act 1950 — Admissibility without Section 90A(2) certificate — Oral evidence of system owner (SP1) and Investigating Officer (SP5) establishing ordinary use and good working order — Permissive nature of Section 90A(2) (“may be proved”) — Application of Ahmad Najib Aris v PP, Hanafi Mat Hassan v PP, and Mohd Azmi Ibrahim v PP — Minor discrepancy in mode of video transmission (WhatsApp vs pen-drive) — Whether affecting chain of custody or authenticity. EVIDENCE: Identification Evidence — Visual identification — Masked perpetrator — Investigating officer (SP5) identifying accused from CCTV recording (Exhibit P12) and photo (Exhibit P4) based on physical build and facial features (“wajah”) — Investigating officer not an eyewitness — Suspect wearing face mask at all times — Inherent impossibility and unreliability of identifying facial features of a masked intruder — Failure of trial judge to apply Turnbull guidelines (R v Turnbull, Duis Akim v PP) — Whether identification evidence of good quality — Necessity for independent corroborative evidence proving visual identification was not mistaken. EVIDENCE: Circumstantial Evidence — Fingerprint evidence — Fingerprint impressions (J1, J2, J3) lifted solely from external automatic gate exposed to public access — Absence of fingerprints from point of forced entry (window/grille) or interior of house (locus of theft) — Distinction from cases where prints found on interior objects (Ng Boon Soon v PP) — Whether fingerprints on an outer gate sufficient to place accused inside dwelling or verify identity as masked intruder — Failure to satisfy "irresistible conclusion" test (Karam Singh v PP, Ermiadi v PP). CRIMINAL PROCEDURE: Appeal — Function and duty of appellate court — Section 316(b)(i) Criminal Procedure Code — Re-evaluation of evidence — Maximum evaluation standard — Section 173(m)(i) & Section 182A Criminal Procedure Code — Duty of trial court to evaluate whole evidence at close of defence case (Nagappan Subramaniam v PP, Mat v PP, Amri Ibrahim v PP) — Prima facie finding not synonymous with proof beyond reasonable doubt — Reversal of conviction and sentence — Safety of conviction — Acquittal and discharge.

judgments.title: MKD SIGNATURE SDN. BHD. v MULIA INTERNATIONAL LIMITED
judgments.catchwords: Tun Razak Exchange Tower (“Exchange 106”)-stay application-Articles 26, 36 and 41 of the ICSID Convention-International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes [“ICSID”]-Convention for the Settlement of Investment Disputes between States and Nationals of Other States [“ICSID Convention”] [“ICSID Arbitration”]-Schedule of the Convention on the Settlement of Investment Disputes Act 1996 [“ICSID Act”]-section 10 of the Arbitration Act 2005-Article 26 of the ICSID Convention gives the ICSID exclusive jurisdiction over the disputes-distinction between contract claims and treaty claims-principle of attribution-exclusive jurisdiction of the Malaysian Courts-ASEAN Comprehensive Investment Agreement 2009-grant a stay under its inherent jurisdiction or under its case management power-statement by counsel from the Bar-a court faced with a claim that may call for arbitration under ICSID must stay the domestic proceedings pending determination by the ICSID Secretary General or arbitral tribunal, lest Malaysia-Parties in the ICSID arbitration are different from the parties in the Court suit-Reliefs prayed for in the ICSID arbitration by Eka are different from the contractual reliefs sought by the plaintiff in the Court suit-No overlap of issues and inconsistent decisions-64. Article 26 of the ICSID Convention states as follows:“Consent of the parties to arbitration under this Convention shall, unless otherwise stated, be deemed consent to such arbitration to the exclusion of any other remedy. A Contracting State may require the exhaustion of local administrative or judicial remedies as a condition of its consent to arbitration under this Convention.”-an application of the court’s wide inherent powers to manage proceedings before the court-test to stay proceedings pending another court’s proceeding, pending an appeal from that court or pending other arbitral proceedings-Special circumstances-prevent injustice and abuse of court process-the determination of stay applications requires an exercise of balancing many of the ingredients enshrined in the overriding objective: the avoidance of excessive cost, the unnecessary expenditure of finite public resources, the right of every litigant to expeditious justice, the minimising of litigation delays, managing the interface and overlap between two judicial organisations, the allocation of limited judicial resources and, broadly, the convenience of all concerned. Fairness, reasonableness and proportionality loom large in the balancing exercise-Decisions of ICSID tribunals have recognised that arbitrations under ICSID can run concurrently with court proceedings or contractual arbitration proceedings between the parties-parallel proceedings

judgments.title: Pendakwa Raya & ors v Julasiri Bin Akilmara
judgments.catchwords: Offence under section 39B(1)(a) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 read together with section 34 of the Penal Code - Whether the trial judge should have informed at the close of the prosecution's case, that the defence was being called upon to answer a case of actual trafficking or presumed trafficking? - Overwhelming evidence proved the elements of custody, control, and knowledge - Actual possession of the impugned drugs was established - Section 180 (1) and (4) of the Criminal Procedure Code - Procedure after conclusion of case for prosecution - No statutory or legal requirement to state the presumption when calling for the defence - Formal verbal label for an evidentiary rule at the close of the prosecution's case is unnecessary - Statutory presumption of trafficking under section 37(da)(xvi) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 - Section 422 of the Criminal Procedure Code - Not vitiate the conviction - No miscarriage of justice - Failure either to make or to record such a finding does not ipso facto - The law does not require a mini-judgment or detailed legal reasons at the close of the prosecution’s case
